It is a leading disputed shrine for the Shikinaisha "Iwakurawake-no-Mikoto Shrine." It is said to be a merger ({{ill|Co-Enshrinement|ja|合祀|qid=Q11412524}}) of '''Kinomiya Shrine''' into the '''Hachimangū''' that originally stood at this location. Under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=modern shrine ranking system}}, each was separately designated as a {{ill|Gō-sha|ja|郷社|qid=Q134917316}}, a rare example. {{nihongo|'''Hachimangū Kinomiya Shrine'''|八幡宮来宮神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Izu Province]].

== Shrine name ==
'''Hachimangū''' is said to be the origin of the place name "Yawatano," and '''Kinomiya Shrine''' was formerly also written as "Ki no Miya" (木宮, "tree shrine").

== Enshrined deities ==
*{{ill|Emperor Ōjin|Q317997|qid=Q317997|lt=Honda Wake-no-Mikoto}} (Hachimangū) — said to have been the {{ill|Landlord deity|Q4160872|qid=Q4160872}} (land deity) of this location from the beginning.
*Iwakurawake-no-Mikoto (いわくらわけのみこと) (Kinomiya Shrine) — because originally enshrined in a rock cave, the name is thought to mean "deity of the {{ill|Iwakura rock|Q11587880|qid=Q11587880}} (sacred rock)." The deity was reputed to be an extreme lover of sake.

The name "Ki (Tree) no Miya" of Kinomiya Shrine, legends of a drifting deity, and other features show strong characteristics of {{ill|Kinomiya Faith|Q11296898|qid=Q11296898}}.

== History ==
According to shrine tradition, '''Hachimangū''' was invited (kanjō) in {{ill|Jingo-keiun|Q1373049|qid=Q1373049}} 3 ({{ill|769|Q30697|qid=Q30697}}) under a system of establishing one Hachimangū per province, and was designated as the Hachimangū of {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|Q317997|qid=Q317997|lt=Izu Province}}. '''Kinomiya Shrine''' is said to have drifted ashore in ancient times, carried on a jar, to a place called Kongōne-zu near Yawatano Port, east of the present location; it was enshrined in a rock cave called "Dō no Ana" and later transferred to Hachimangū. Furthermore, it is said that the two shrines were originally in separate halls, but during the {{ill|Enryaku|Q1373176|qid=Q1373176}} era (782–806) they came to be enshrined together in a single main hall. Because Kinomiya Shrine's enshrined deity is Iwakurawake-no-Mikoto, it is identified as the Shikinaisha "Iwakurawake-no-Mikoto Shrine," and is also identified with the "Ju-shi-i-jō Iwakurawake-no-Myōjin" (Senior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade) recorded in the '{{ill|Izumi Province Divine Name Register|Q11420490|qid=Q11420490|lt=Izu Provincial Deity Rank Record}}' bearing a {{ill|Kōei|Q980266|qid=Q980266}} 2 ({{ill|1343|Q6072|qid=Q6072}}) colophon.

In Meiji 6 ({{ill|1873|Q7757|qid=Q7757}}), '''Hachimangū''' was ranked as a gōsha, and in Meiji 9, '''Kinomiya Shrine''' was also elevated to gōsha. After the war, it belongs to the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077}}.

== Legends ==
*The deity of Kinomiya had such a great love of sake that when enshrined near the coast, he would demand sake offerings from ships passing offshore; the troubled people moved the deity inland to a corner of the current shrine grounds called "Motoyashiki," but the sea was still visible from there and the deity continued demanding sake, so he was moved a second time to beside the Hachimangū.
*In the age of gods, when the deities gathered to divide the rivers, the Kinomiya deity fell asleep drunk and was left with only the muddy river of Naramato, where {{ill|Atagawa Onsen|Q11569041|qid=Q11569041}} is located; the deity disliked it and refused to take it. This is said to explain why the Yawatano area is poorly supplied with water and has no hot springs<ref>Kimura Hiroshi, "Kinomiya Shrine, Hachimangū Kinomiya Shrine, Sugihoko-wake-no-Mikoto Shrine" (in 'Nihon no Kamigami — Jinja to Seichi')</ref>.

== Rituals ==
*Annual festival ({{ill|September 15|Q2846|qid=Q2846}}) — after the annual festival, the mikoshi processes to a temporary resting place (kariya) set up on the beach, stays one night, and returns the following {{ill|September 16|Q2897|qid=Q2897|lt=16th}}. In former times, sacred sake was placed in bamboo tubes and sent to {{ill|Ikonahime no Mikoto Shrine|Q11379183|qid=Q11379183}}.

== Shrine buildings ==
*Honden (main hall) — two-bay, one-bay-deep {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684|qid=Q210684}} with copper-plate roofing, reconstructed in {{ill|Kansei|Q1195131|qid=Q1195131}} 7 ({{ill|1795|Q7815|qid=Q7815}}). Honda Wake-no-Mikoto is enshrined on the right (as viewed) and Iwakurawake-no-Mikoto on the left, creating a rare two-bay nagare-zukuri form.
*Haiden (worship hall) — three-bay front, two-bay side, {{ill|East Asian hip-and-gable roof|Q855025|qid=Q855025}} with copper-plate roofing, with a one-bay {{ill|kōhai|Q11415970|qid=Q11415970}} (front porch). Reconstructed in {{ill|Bunsei|Q1327119|qid=Q1327119}} 7 ({{ill|1824|Q6994|qid=Q6994}}).
The main hall and worship hall are connected by a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=ryōsage-zukuri}} corridor hall (heiden); these three structures are designated cultural properties of Shizuoka Prefecture.

== Auxiliary shrines ==
Tenshō Kōtaijingū, Toyouke Kōtaijingū, Ōkuninushi Shrine, Wakamiya Hachimangū, Tenmangū, Ebisu Shrine, Koyasu Shrine, Akiba-gū, Hitaki Shrine, Sui Shrine

== Cultural properties ==
== Natural monument (nationally designated) ==
*{{ill|Yawatano Hachimangū/Kinomiya Shrine sacred grove|Q124367794|qid=Q124367794}} — a typical lucidophyll forest where tall trees such as {{ill|Quercus salicina|Q4111865|qid=Q4111865}}, {{ill|Quercus glauca|Q714124|qid=Q714124}}, {{ill|Quercus gilva|Q3414213|qid=Q3414213}}, {{ill|Castanopsis sieboldii|Q846994|qid=Q846994}}, and {{ill|Machilus thunbergii|Q5792073|qid=Q5792073}} are entwined with vines such as {{ill|Uncaria rhynchophylla|Q1134307|qid=Q1134307}}, with fern colonies below. In particular, the colony of {{ill|Angiopteris lygodiifolia|Q15251683|qid=Q15251683}} is considered the northernmost natural habitat in the Japanese archipelago. Designated as a natural monument in 1934 (Shōwa 9).

== Shizuoka Prefecture designated tangible cultural properties ==
*Hachimangū Kinomiya Shrine Honden, Watadono, and Haiden

== Itō City designated cultural properties ==
*Hachimangū Kinomiya Shrine mikoshi (2 units) — repaired in {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=An'ei}} 7 ({{ill|1778|Q7713|qid=Q7713}}).
*Hachimangū Kinomiya Shrine yatai float

== Other ==
Inside "Dō no Ana," the former site of Kinomiya Shrine, stand small shrines and stone Buddhist images called "{{ill|Awashima-no-Kami|Q1575740|qid=Q1575740}}" and "{{ill|Inari Ōkami|abstract|Q719665|ar|إناري|az|İnari Okami|ban|Inari (Kami)|bcl|Inari Ōkami|ca|Oinari|cs|Inari (mytologie)|da|Inari|de|Inari (Kami)|el|Ινάρι Όκαμι|es|Inari (Japón)|et|Inari (jumal)|eu|Inari Ōkami|fa|ایناری|fi|Inari (kami)|fr|Inari (divinité japonaise)|hr|Inari|hu|Inari (sintó)|hy|Ինարի Օկամի|id|Inari (Kami)|it|Inari (mitologia)|ja|稲荷神|jv|Inari (Kami)|ko|이나리노카미|mni|ꯏꯅꯔꯤ ꯑꯣꯀꯃꯤ|ne|इनारी ओकामी|nl|Inari Ōkami|no|Inari|pl|Inari (bóstwo)|pt|Inari Ōkami|ru|Инари (божество)|simple|Inari Ōkami|sl|Inari (mitologija)|sr|Инари (богиња)|sv|Inari|tok|jan sewi suli Inali|tr|Inari Ōkami|uk|Інарі (міфологія)|vi|Inari Ōkami|zh|稻荷神|qid=Q719665}}." The former Yawatano area consisted of two hamlets: the hillside "Oka" (agriculture-based) and the coastal "Hama" (fishing-based). Women of the Hama hamlet would seclude themselves in this cave during childbirth and menstruation, revering "Awashima-sama" as a deity of women's ailments and childbirth. Also, people of this area carried loads on their heads, a custom said to have been at nearly the northernmost limit on the {{ill|Pacific Ocean|Q98|qid=Q98}} coast of the {{ill|Japanese archipelago|Q841337|qid=Q841337}}.
